original.guitar: Acoustic rhythm guitar (band guitarists over the years include Gilles Cartin, André Marchand and Michel Bordeleau; track credits not found)
original.amp: Acoustic instrument
original.effects: None (acoustic folk recording)
original.notes: Traditional Quebec music: accordion, fiddle, foot-tapping (podorythmie) and acoustic guitar. The album and players on this track were not confirmed.

recipes.tips: In Quebec trad music the guitar is the rhythm section: strong, percussive strumming that locks in with the foot-tapping, with accents on the off-beats and bass notes alternating on the downbeats. Channel A is brighter and more percussive, channel B a bit warmer. Leave the melody to the accordion and fiddle.
recipes.why: The guitar on these recordings is acoustic. The ACOUSTIC effect into a very clean amp, with a short room reverb, gets an electric close to a strummed acoustic. The brighter treble setting helps the strumming cut through accordion and fiddle.

original.amp: Not applicable (acoustic arrangement)
original.effects: None
original.notes: For playing the song with a plain electric sound instead of the acoustic simulation.

recipes.tips: Channel A is a plain, clean electric for percussive strumming. Channel B is a warmer AC15 with a touch of grit. There's no delay, so fast strumming stays tight: add the slapback (DELAY) only if the room sounds dead.
recipes.why: If you'd rather sound like an electric guitar, a clean, lightly compressed amp with a short room reverb keeps the fast trad rhythm crisp and out of the way of the accordion and fiddle.

original.guitar: Patrick Bourgeois or Alain Lapointe (the credits for this track were not found)
original.amp: Unknown. Typical early-90s Quebec pop-rock studio sound: clean, compressed, chorus and stereo delay
original.effects: Chorus, stereo delay, plate/hall reverb (era style, not documented)
original.notes: From the album Snob (1991). No source documents the gear on this song, so this tone follows the style of the record.

recipes.tips: Channel A for the clean, chorused verses. Switch to channel B for a light AC30 crunch in the choruses. Stomp COMP for more sustain on arpeggios. The chorus and delay are stereo: they sound widest if the mixer has the Tonelab's L and R outputs panned apart.
recipes.why: The early-90s pop-rock clean sound is a bright clean amp with chorus, a stereo delay just under the beat and a plate reverb. Both pickups, split, give a glassy, Strat-like middle-position sound.

original.amp: Unknown. Typical modern-country clean: Fender-style amp, compressed
original.effects: Compressor, slapback delay, spring reverb (genre style, not documented)
original.notes: From This One's for You (2017), produced by Scott Moffatt. No source documents the gear, so this tone follows the style of the record.

recipes.tips: Channel A for the clean, twangy fills and chicken-pickin' licks: hybrid-pick (pick plus middle finger) close to the bridge. Switch to channel B for a gritty tweed edge when the band kicks in. The compressor and the 120 ms slapback are what make it sound country, so keep them on.
recipes.why: Modern country electric parts are usually a Telecaster bridge pickup into a clean Fender-style amp, squashed by a compressor, with a short slapback. Pulled (split) Pearly Gates on the bridge is the closest your guitar gets to a Tele bridge pickup.

original.guitar: Billy Sanford (intro riff), with Jerry Kennedy and Wayne Moss doubling it; Roy Orbison also on guitar
original.amp: Not documented. 1964 Nashville session: small tweed/brownface Fender-style amps
original.effects: Studio echo chamber (not documented)
original.notes: Recorded August 1, 1964, produced by Fred Foster, engineered by Bill Porter. Jerry Kennedy suggested starting with one guitar and adding one each time the riff repeats.

recipes.tips: MOD is set to a pitch shifter tuned a few cents sharp and mixed under your guitar. It thickens one guitar into something like the three guitars playing the riff in unison on the record. Turn it off for the very first pass of the riff (one guitar) and on when the others join. Channel A is a rounder Bassman sound, channel B a grittier small tweed. Pick firmly and let the low notes thump.
recipes.why: Mid-60s Nashville sessions used small Fender-style amps turned up just to the edge of breakup, recorded in a studio echo chamber. The record's riff is several guitars in unison, so a slightly detuned copy of your own signal recreates that thickness.

original.notes: From Come On Over (1997), produced by Robert John "Mutt" Lange; guitars tracked at Masterfonics, Nashville.

recipes.tips: Channel A for the main riff: tight JCM900-style crunch on the bridge humbucker. Play it with palm muting and stop the notes sharply, as the riff relies on the gaps. Channel B is a lighter AC30 crunch for the verses. Stomp the Tube OD for an even tighter riff.
recipes.why: Mutt Lange's productions use tight, polished rock guitars, the Def Leppard approach applied to country. A JCM900-style amp gives punch with a firm low end, and a very short delay and a small room keep the riff dry and in your face.

original.guitar: Fender Stratocaster ("Number One"), heavy strings (.013-.058)
original.amp: Two Fender Vibroverbs (one with a 15-inch Altec) and Jackson Browne's Dumble with a 4x12, close-miked with SM57s
original.effects: Ibanez Tube Screamer (the only pedal, per engineer Richard Mullen), amp spring reverb
original.notes: Recorded November 24, 1982 for Texas Flood. Sources differ on how much of each amp is on the record.

recipes.tips: SRV tuned down a half step. Either retune to Eb, or stomp MOD: it's set to a pitch shifter one semitone down so you can play along in standard tuning (expect a little warble). Channel A is the Vibroverb, channel B the Dumble. Dig in hard: the shuffle lives in the picking hand, with muted strings between the chord stabs and the bass-note pattern.
recipes.why: A blackface Fender at the edge of breakup, pushed by a Tube Screamer with low drive and high level, with spring reverb. That's the documented Texas Flood rig. NR is kept low so the dynamics and the muted ghost notes come through.

original.guitar: Fender Stratocaster ("Number One"), heavy strings (.013-.058)
original.amp: Fender Vibroverb and Jackson Browne's Dumble with a 4x12
original.effects: Ibanez Tube Screamer; Roland Dimension D reportedly added to the solo at the mix
original.notes: Recorded November 24, 1982 for Texas Flood.

recipes.tips: Channel A for a brighter Vibroverb solo, channel B for the thicker Dumble one. The slow, shallow stereo chorus stands in for the Roland Dimension D on the record's solo. Turn MOD off for the raw amp sound. Heavy strings and hard picking are half of SRV's tone: play with more attack than feels natural.
recipes.why: Same rig as the rhythm, pushed harder: more amp gain and a bit more Tube Screamer. The Dimension D was a subtle studio widener, so a slow, shallow stereo chorus is the closest thing on the Tonelab.
